official.name: mcp__pixellab__add_to_project
official.description:
Let a game project use a character, object, tileset, map, room or UI asset you
already own, or file an asset (gallery images, tile groups and isometric tiles
too) into a game or folder on the website.
Songs and sound effects go in a game too: the game gets their audio file.

A game gets the asset in its asset library; one not yet in any folder is
also filed under that game. A folder only groups assets on the website: the
asset moves into it and keeps every game it is in. Characters and objects
move with all their states, a UI asset with its elements. Tile groups and
isometric tiles have no asset library to join: they are filed under the
project you name (a tile group reaches a game as a map's tile layer).

A project's game can only load art that belongs to that project, and until
now the only way to put art there was to create it from inside Game Builder.
Art made anywhere else — this MCP server, the website — was invisible to
every game, so the only route was to generate it a second time and pay for
it again.

A saved VFX effect id (My effects, vfx_workbench export) is not linked:
the reply gives its files (game pack with manifest: frame order, timing,
anchor) as download links and the command that puts them in the game.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

official.name: mcp__pixellab__animate_character
official.description:
Queue an animation for a character. Returns job ids at once; ~2-4 min.

Modes (from what you pass; override with `mode`):
- template: template_animation_id, a clip such as walking or breathing-idle.
- v3 (default without a template id): your motion in action_description.
- pixminimax (beta): action_description, clips up to 40 frames, cheap at large sizes.
- skeleton-v3 (beta): a template clip on the character's own skeleton (still
  redrawn each frame, colours hold closer), or without template_animation_id a
  motion you write as poses (the first call returns the format, free).
- template_action: the website's walk/run/sprint/idle and strike animations.

Template and skeleton-v3 animate all the character's directions; v3 and
pixminimax animate south unless you pass directions. To add directions to an
animation, pass its animation_group_id and animation_name. A poor result: delete
it, retry, or try the next mode (template, v3, pixminimax).

Cost: template 1 generation per direction up to ~92px (more above; the receipt
gives the ceiling). v3 ceil(w*h*frames/65536) per direction on the generated
canvas (64px at 8 frames = 1, 96-128px = 2-3). pixminimax 1-6 per direction by
size and frames. skeleton-v3 2-4 per direction.

Cancel a pending or processing background job.

Releases the concurrency slot immediately so you can start new work.
Already-completed or already-failed jobs are left unchanged.

Cost: work that has not started costs nothing to cancel, but a job already
generating is billed for the work done — an image request already sent
usually costs its full price — and an earlier batch of an animation stays
billed. Without "generation stopped" in the reply, work running in another
process may still finish and charge; get_image on the job then names the
saved result. A job that fails on its own is never charged, and one that
completed cannot be cancelled: its charge stands.

official.description:
Queue a state (variant) of an existing character. The new character keeps
the source's identity, body type, and proportions, with the edit applied
consistently across all 4 or 8 rotations. Auto-waits up to 30s for the
source to complete.

A character is a group of states: `name` is the character's name (shared by
all states), and each state has its own `state_name` — defaulting to the
edit description truncated to 20 characters (a new character's first state
is named "Idle"). Pass `state_name` to name the new state explicitly.

IMPORTANT — this ALWAYS preserves the SAME individual's face and identity,
even for edits like "elderly", "wounded", or a different class/role. It makes
a variant OF this character (different outfit/pose/state), NOT a new character.
To make a DIFFERENT character in the same art style, use create_character with
matching size/view/outline/shading/detail params (and a v3 reference image if
you want to match the look) — not create_character_state.

Returns a new character_id grouped with the source via group_id. Inspect
sibling states with `get_character` on either id.

`palette` (hex colours, plus `palette_name`) puts every direction of the state on
those colours, the source's rotations first; it can't be combined with
use_color_palette_from_reference (max_colors alone can).

Cost: ONE charge for the whole state — every rotation the source has, 4 or 8,
is redrawn and billed together, so there is no per-direction price and an
8-direction character costs the same as a 4-direction one. It is 10, 15 or 25
generations, set by the size of the character's own ART rather than its
canvas. The rotations' content is squared, padded 20% and
floored at 32px; that cell costs 10 up to 84px, 15 from 85 to 112, 25 above.
The art cannot be bigger than the frame, so a character whose frames are
70px or smaller ALWAYS costs 10 (a 48x48 character is 10), and one up to
93px never costs more than 15. Setting override_width/override_height is the
exception: an enlarged state is priced on the NEW frame size directly, art
or no art, against the same 84/112 thresholds — so enlarging a 48x48
character to 128x128 turns a 10 into a 25. Only above that is the charge genuinely
unknown before the call, because it depends on how much of the frame the art
fills; the balance check reserves only the 10 floor, so a call there CAN
charge more than it reserved — leave 25 of headroom or check get_balance.

official.description:
Create an empty map seeded with a tileset and everything connected to it,
or with a tile group.

The map starts with no painted cells — paint it with edit_map, which grows
the bounds as you go. Tile size comes from the seed tileset. A map started
from a tile group is a tile map instead: its tiles go on tile layers with
place_map_tiles, which can stack them. A map started from a sidescroller
tileset is a sidescroller map: paint the solid ground with edit_map, and it
gets a background preset as in Map Workshop.

top-down map. Returns a tileset id at once; poll get_topdown_tileset (standard

mcp__pixellab__create_vocal_animation
official.description:
Generate a talking mouth-position set ("visemes") for a character's portrait.

Produces one keyframe per mouth shape, all sharing the chosen expression, so
the character can be lip-synced to any line of text afterwards. Building the
set costs generations ONCE; turning it into talking animations with
create_talking_gif is free.

Works two ways. With `character_id` the set is saved onto that character, so
every later call needs only the id — use this when the character exists.
With `image` you generate straight from a portrait and nothing is stored; the
frames live in the job for 8 hours and you reference it by job id.

Cost: 3 generations for the default 7 mouth positions on a portrait up to
64px. Two things scale it — the position count sets how many drawing passes
run (2 passes for 3 positions, 3 for 5 or 7, 4 for 12) and the portrait's size
sets what one pass costs (1 generation up to 64px, 2 at 96-128px, 4 at 160px,
5 at 192px, 8 at 256px). So 7 positions is 3 at 64px, 6 at 128px and 24 at
256px, while 12 positions on a 64px portrait is 4. engine="pixminimax" prices
a pass at 1 generation at every size, so a big portrait is far cheaper there.
A set can need a few extra passes to fill in a position, so the figure in the
submit receipt is the one to quote; those extra passes stop once a call
reaches 40 generations, which is the ceiling for any size and count. Turning
the set into talking animations with create_talking_gif is free, however many
lines you lip-sync.

Requires a subscription (or trial). The character form needs a portrait set
first. To delete an expression again:
set_character_portrait(character_id, remove_expression="angry").

Examples:
- Default talking set for a character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>")
- Add an angry expression to the same character:
  create_vocal_animation(character_id="<uuid>", mood="angry")
- Just a portrait, no character:
  create_vocal_animation(image=<portrait_png>)

Generation time: ~2-5 minutes (async processing)

```ts
declare const tools: { mcp__pixellab__create_vocal_animation(args: {
  // Character to generate the expression for; it must already have a portrait, and the finished set is saved onto it so later calls only need the character id. Mutually exclusive with `image`.
  character_id?: string | null;
  // Which generator draws the mouth positions. 'v3' (default) is the original one. 'pixminimax' (PixMiniMax, beta) keeps the eyes, brows and head still while only the mouth moves, and costs the same at every portrait size up to 256px: 3 generations for 7 positions (2 for 3, 4 for 12), where v3 costs 3 at 64px, 6 at 128px and 24 at 256px.
  engine?: "v3" | "pixminimax";
  // Generate from this portrait PNG (base64) instead, without a character. Nothing is stored: the mouth positions come back from get_vocal_animation and you pass that job id to create_talking_gif. Use this when the user only has a portrait. Mutually exclusive with `character_id`. Max 256x256.
  image?: string | null;
  // Expression baked into the face (brows/eyes/cheeks). The mouth shapes are the same across moods. One call per mood; each is stored as its own row of the character's vocal grid.
  mood?: "neutral" | "happy" | "angry" | "sad" | "surprised";
  // Cut out the background so frames are transparent PNGs — usually what you want for compositing over a game scene.
  no_background?: boolean;
  // Seed for reproducible generation.
  seed?: number | null;
  // How many mouth positions to generate. 3 = minimal (tiny portraits), 5 = basic, 7 = recommended, 12 = high quality (large close-ups). Must match across moods for the same character.
  viseme_count?: 3 | 5 | 7 | 12;
}): Promise<CallToolResult>; };
```

official.description:
Estimate the skeleton of a humanoid sprite: its 18 joints, in exactly the
shape animate_with_skeleton_v3 takes.

Two calls: estimate_skeleton(image=...) queues it and returns a job id (usually
done in ~10-20 s, longer when the queue is busy); estimate_skeleton(job_id=...)
returns the keypoints once it is done (wait_for_jobs waits for it).

Pass the result as animate_with_skeleton_v3's `first_frame_keypoints` (the pose
the sprite is in), and use it as the starting point for each frame of
`keypoints` (the motion: move the joints frame by frame). x/y are fractions 0-1
of the image you sent; labels come in the order animate_with_skeleton_v3

official.description:
Get character details, rotation URLs, animations, and download link.
Branches by status: processing (progress+ETA), failed (error+retry), completed (full data).

group — `?states=` narrows it, taking the state IDS this tool prints on

animation-direction, uniform cells sized to the largest frame with the rest

official.name: mcp__pixellab__move_map_object
mcp__pixellab__pixelart_workbench
official.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,…] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours, to LOOK at: the id it returns still holds the whole
  picture, so passing it on sends the full canvas and not the region.
  `split … --count` below is what actually cuts a piece out
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 [--count n] — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an
  animation, one frame per cell (columns x rows). --count keeps the first n
  cells and drops the rest, so `split <image> --grid 2x1 --count 1` is the
  free exact crop of the left half, `--grid 1x2 --count 1` the top half, and
  a one-cell result downloads as image.png (a multi-frame one has no
  image.png, only frames.png — which is why a plain 2x1 split cannot be
  handed on as a single picture). Cells must divide the canvas evenly; the
  error names the counts that fit. Without --count, trailing cells that are
  one flat colour are dropped
- join <image> <image> … [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[…]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{…}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.

official.description:
Downscale upscaled pixel art back onto its true pixel grid.

Pixel art found online is almost always scaled up — a 32x32 sprite saved at
512x512, where every art pixel is a 16x16 block. Every tool that takes a
reference or style image works far better on the real 32x32 sprite, and this
recovers it: the pixel grid is detected and the image is downsampled onto it.

you are about to pass it to create_image_pixflux(init_image), a style image,
edit_image, or create_character. If the art was never upscaled it is already

picture, redrawing it. This one only downscales art that is already pixel art.
